questions.prompt: CI builds the same commit twice with the same Dockerfile and gets two different image IDs. What changed?
choices: The base image was updated between builds
Timestamps: COPY keeps the files' modification times and the config records a creation time, so the layer bytes and the config bytes differ even though the content is the same
Docker adds a random nonce to every build
The image ID includes the build host name
questions.explanation: An image ID is the SHA-256 of the config, which embeds the diff_ids of the layers. Any byte that differs, including the mtime stored for every tar entry and the created timestamp, changes it. Fixed timestamps (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, rewrite-timestamp) make the build reproducible.

questions.prompt: A layer has a diff_id and a digest. Which is which?
choices: diff_id is the compressed blob, digest is the uncompressed tar
diff_id is the SHA-256 of the uncompressed tar and lives in the config; digest is the SHA-256 of the compressed blob and lives in the manifest
They are the same value in two places
diff_id is per file, digest is per layer
questions.explanation: The daemon identifies layers by their uncompressed content, registries by the compressed blob they store. Recompressing a layer changes its digest but not its diff_id, which is why the same image ID can appear under several manifest digests.

questions.prompt: Two images put an identical app layer on top of different base images. Why does the daemon not share that layer between them?
choices: It does; layers are always shared by diff_id
Layers in position are identified by chain ID, the hash of the previous chain ID and this diff_id, so the same diff_id on a different parent is a different chain ID
Because the tags differ
Because the config differs
questions.explanation: A layer's content only makes sense on top of what is below it. The chain ID encodes the whole stack, so the layer store can reuse 'alpine + app' for every image that has exactly that prefix, and only those.

questions.prompt: mkimage prints an `image id` before `docker load` ever runs. What did it hash?
choices: The manifest
The config JSON, which includes the diff_ids, the entrypoint, the environment and the timestamps
The concatenated layers
The tag
questions.explanation: The image ID is the digest of the config blob. Docker's classic store shows exactly this value as IMAGE ID; the containerd image store (default since Docker 29) shows the manifest digest there instead, which is a different value that covers the compressed layers and is what name@sha256:… pulls.

questions.prompt: mkimage writes an OCI layout and a legacy manifest.json into one tarball. Why both?
choices: The OCI layout is for Docker and manifest.json is for Podman
Both describe the same blobs: index.json is what registries, skopeo, crane and recent daemons read, manifest.json is what older docker load reads, so one archive works everywhere
manifest.json holds the layers and index.json holds the config
It is required by the OCI specification
questions.explanation: The blobs are the image; the two indexes are two tables of contents. docker save has emitted both since Docker 25 for the same compatibility reason.

questions.prompt: A Dockerfile with COPY, RUN rm /etc/motd, ENV and ENTRYPOINT produces how many filesystem layers on top of the base, and what do ENV and ENTRYPOINT produce?
choices: Four layers; every instruction is a layer
Two layers (COPY and the RUN whiteout); ENV and ENTRYPOINT change only the config and appear as empty_layer history rows
One layer; Docker squashes them
Three layers; ENTRYPOINT has no layer but ENV does
questions.explanation: Only instructions that change the filesystem produce layers. Metadata instructions edit the config and leave a history row flagged empty_layer, which is why the Image Layers auditor skips them when matching history to layers.
